Approved Howard-to-Solstice line closes in on Uvalde

New route implicates city structures, farmland
By Hali Mecklin
on September 17, 2026

Staff writer Hali Mecklin
Uvalde Leader-News
FacebookTwitterEmailMessengerCopy LinkMessageShare
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:39
Instaread

The Public Utility Commission of Texas approved the Howard-to-Solstice 765-kilovolt Transmission Line on Sept. 11, and moved its route closer to Uvalde’s city limits in a reported effort to reduce environmental impacts and preserve views of the Hill Country.

The high-voltage, 370-mile line will cross Highway 83 about 1.5 miles north of the city. It will also cross Highway 55 North, and run parallel to West Farm-to-Market Road 2369 before crossing the Nueces River. Fifteen more Uvalde structures are implicated by the new route, meaning the power line could cross the owners’ property.

“It does go closer to the city [of Uvalde], so that will implicate additional structures, but… landowners can work with utilities and hopefully reduce those impacts,” said commissioner Courtney Hjaltman, who proposed the approved deviation from Route 4.

The line, a joint AEP Texas and CPS Energy project, will bring electricity from South Texas to the Permian Basin to power oil production. Other affected counties include Atascosa, Bandera, Bexar, Crockett, Edwards, Kerr, Kinney, Medina, Pecos, Real, Sutton, Terrell and Val Verde.

Local community members, officials and coalitions have voiced concerns about the transmission line for more than a year. They worry about environmental impact and the rights of private landowners. Uvalde County Commissioners unanimously approved a resolution opposing the transmission line on Oct. 14, 2025. Precinct 3 commissioner Roy Kothmann, who also serves on the Border Sub-Regional Planning Commission, said he is against the project regardless of its route.

“We don’t need an extension cord going across our county,” he told the newspaper.

Kothmann has spoken to several of the 15 households directly affected by the lines, and landowners across the county whose views will now be obstructed by electrical towers. He said he can appreciate PUCT commissioners’ reluctance to scar virgin landscapes, but it will be at the expense of over a dozen Uvalde stakeholders. He suggested the state invest in natural-gas generation to get power to West Texas — an idea AEP dismissed as not economically viable, according to Kothmann.

“If the state wants to preserve its beauty… maybe they could help provide new generation out there,” he said, referring to Midland. “They provide tax incentives for data centers, and they’re the ones using all this electricity anyways.”

Kothmann believes county residents will reap “no benefit” from the lines. Customers could actually see their bills increase due to rising transmission costs jacking up energy rates statewide, according to the Texas Public Policy Foundation.

Sabinal Mayor Erik Gomez is also a member of the Border Sub-Regional Planning Commission, and a vocal opponent of the sprawling transmission lines. While the Howard-to-Solstice line won’t run through Sabinal, which is 20 miles east of Uvalde, it will implicate land several miles south of the town.

“It broke my heart… I just feel so sorry for [affected landowners]. What I’m hoping is the state legislature can convene and try to slow it down or stop it.” Gomez said of the project. “Some of Sabinal’s biggest economy is hunting and farming, and some of our biggest ranches are gonna get affected by it.”

The mayor, who is also a U.S. Border Patrol agent, raised concerns about smugglers and narco-traffickers using structures along the transmission line. He believes they could serve as a guide or reference point from the U.S.-Mexico border to Texas cities.
“The cartels, they’re gonna love this new tool they have,” he said.

Hjaltman acknowledged landowners’ frustrations at the Sept. 11 PUCT meeting.

“You’ve shared your comments, you’ve shared your stories, you’ve told us about your land, your families, your heritage, and those perspectives really did matter,” Hjaltman said. “My goal in making these changes was to reduce the impacts where possible by encouraging greater use of existing corridors, and really minimizing the destruction of land.”

Committee Chairman Thomas Gleeson directed AEP on Sept. 11 to work with landowners and minimize impact. Stephanie Houle, the company’s vice president of regulatory affairs, said AEP Texas will “accept accountability.”

Construction is scheduled to begin fall 2028 and complete in 2031, according to AEP’s website. The typical transmission line structure along the Howard-to-Solstice route will stand 140 to 160 feet tall, with a right-of-way width of 200 feet. The structures will sit 1,400 feet apart from one another.

Texas external affair manager Jimmy Earnest said AEP had not received PUCT’s official approval in writing as of Sept. 13, and could not yet answer questions about costs, next steps or impacts on Uvalde homeowners.
